roleTitle: Operations Process Specialist, Equipment Maintenance Services
jobDescription: The maintenance services division of an industrial equipment supplier dispatches field technicians to customer sites for planned maintenance and breakdown repairs. The Operations Process Specialist owns the work-order intake and scheduling procedure, maintains the parts-request checklist, coordinates with the regional depots on parts availability, and is expected to cut the number of repeat visits caused by missing parts, reported against a defined baseline.
requirements: Runs the work-order intake and scheduling procedure for planned maintenance and breakdown repairs.
Maintains the parts-request checklist used by dispatchers and technicians.
Cuts the number of repeat visits caused by missing parts, reported against a defined baseline and period.
Coordinates parts availability with the regional depots and records own responsibility boundaries.
Documents known limitations and hand-over conditions at the end of each scheduling week.

evidence.text: Ran work-order intake and scheduling for two regional service teams in the field-service system, assigning planned maintenance and breakdown jobs to technicians and re-sequencing the day when a breakdown came in.
Maintained the parts-request checklist that dispatchers complete before a visit is confirmed, adding a step to confirm depot stock for the top twenty part numbers.
Coordinated parts availability with the three regional depots by phone and the depot stock report each morning; stock transfers between depots were approved by the depot supervisors.
Wrote the weekly scheduling hand-over for the incoming dispatcher, listing open work orders, parts still on order and jobs that needed a second visit.
Responsibilities included work-order intake, scheduling, parts-request checklist maintenance and depot coordination for about eighteen months in the maintenance services division.

Work sample: the parts-request checklist with the depot-stock step and one weekly scheduling hand-over listing open work orders and parts on order, with the field-service system's work-order numbers as a verification trail.

Reference call with former dispatch supervisor: said the checklist change 'made a real difference' and that repeat visits 'went down a lot, maybe by a third'; she could not recall whether anyone had measured it and said the division did not track repeat-visit reasons at the time.

Hiring manager pre-read: the service director has asked for a specialist who can demonstrate a measured reduction in repeat visits, so please be clear in the packet about what is measured and what is remembered.

propositions.text: The candidate ran work-order intake and scheduling for two regional service teams in the field-service system.
propositions.rationale: The resume describes the intake and scheduling work directly.

propositions.text: The candidate maintained the parts-request checklist and added a depot-stock confirmation step for the top twenty part numbers.
propositions.rationale: The resume and the checklist work sample document the change.

propositions.text: The candidate's checklist change reduced repeat visits caused by missing parts by a third.
propositions.rationale: The only figure is a referee's recollection with no measurement; the referee states that repeat-visit reasons were not tracked at the time.

gold.expectedGap: No measurement, baseline or period in the materials links a reduction in repeat visits to the candidate's checklist change.
gold.expectedBoundaryNote: Keep the referee's recollection as an unmeasured impression; the materials document the checklist change itself, not its effect.
followUpTargets: Ask whether repeat-visit reasons were ever tracked, and for any depot or service report that shows repeat visits before and after the checklist change.
